decisions.final:
Matching a described monitoring practice to the correct measure for understanding (tracking) intraday flows.

The reading lists five measures for tracking intraday flows. Each is distinguished by what is being recorded:

| Measure | What it captures |
|---|---|
| Total payments | Statistics on the amount of payments: payer and payee information, the payment system used, the time received or originated, routing information, any suspensions, and the credit status of the payment |
| Other cash transactions | Intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at all financial market utilities (FMUs) in which the bank participates, maximising transaction-level detail and capturing the data for analysis |
| Time-sensitive obligations | Transactions that must be completed by a specific time during the day |
| Total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties | The intraday lines the bank has extended |
| Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage | The intraday lines extended to the bank, and how much of them it uses |

The stem matches the reading's definition of other cash transactions word for word: settlement positions, at every FMU, at transaction level, stored for analysis. The name is counter-intuitive, which is exactly why it is tested: the measure is labelled other cash transactions but is organised by venue (the FMU) rather than by individual payment. 'Settlement positions' is the content of that measure, not a separately named measure.

Why it is tracked separately from total payments: a bank's settlement position at a given utility can be its largest intraday exposure at that venue and can flip between a receipt and an obligation from day to day, so folding it into total payments would conceal the concentration.

decisions.final:
The distinction between measures that describe intraday activity and measures that size the resulting exposure.

The two families answer different questions, and every question on this material turns on keeping them apart.

| | Tracking (understanding) intraday flows | Quantifying and monitoring risk levels |
|---|---|---|
| Question answered | What moved through the bank today, and what lines exist | How much exposure did that activity create |
| Members | Total payments; other cash transactions (settlement positions at each FMU); time-sensitive obligations; total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties; total bank intraday credit lines available and usage | Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage; intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital; client intraday credit usage; payment throughput |
| Character | Descriptive; records amounts, positions and lines | Evaluative; each measure is a peak, a ratio, or a comparison against a limit, capital or time of day |

The structural tell is the comparison. A risk measure sets something against something else: a client's peak overdraft against the established line, intraday credit against Tier 1 capital, outgoing payment activity against time of day. A flow measure simply records. If the measure has a denominator, it belongs to the second family.

The credit-line totals are the members most often misfiled, because credit feels like exposure. Total intraday credit lines (to clients, or available to the bank and used) simply record the lines, so they are flow measures, whereas client intraday credit usage compares a peak overdraft against the line and is a risk measure.

decisions.final:
Distinguishing the measures used to quantify and monitor intraday risk, and separating them from the credit-line totals used to track flows, by whose position each one measures.

The measures are separated by whose exposure they capture and against what the figure is compared. Getting the actor right decides most questions on this material.

| Measure | Family | Whose position | Construction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Client intraday credit usage | Risk level | The bank's client | The client's peak daily intraday overdraft compared with the credit line established (committed or uncommitted) for that client |
| Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage | Risk level | The bank's own | The largest net negative position the bank itself reaches during the day |
| Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital | Risk level | The bank's own | Intraday credit scaled by the bank's capital base |
| Payment throughput | Risk level | Operational | The percentage of outgoing payment activity relative to time of day |
| Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage | Flow-tracking | The bank as borrower | Lines extended to the bank, and how much is used |
| Total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties | Flow-tracking | The bank as lender | Lines extended by the bank, in aggregate |

Note the pairing of the last two rows. The bank sits on both sides of the intraday credit market, receiving lines and extending them to its clients, and the two are recorded separately because they fail in opposite directions. A withdrawal of lines to the bank is a funding problem; a drawdown of lines by clients is a credit and liquidity problem. Both are flow-tracking totals; only client intraday credit usage compares a peak overdraft against the line, which is what the stem describes.

Payment throughput is measured for three stated reasons: to track volume patterns and ensure the day's payments are processed on time, to meet financial market utility requirements to submit a target percentage of payments by a deadline, and to identify peak periods and their correlation with intraday liquidity on hand and credit usage.

decisions.final:
The structure of the CFP framework and the boundary between contingency planning and business-as-usual liquidity management.

The framework has five components, each answering a different question about a contingency:

| Component | Question answered |
|---|---|
| Governance and oversight | Who decides, through which committees, with what authority |
| Scenario and liquidity gap analysis | Which events are planned for, and how large is the gap under each |
| Monitoring and escalation | What signals a deteriorating position, and at which level of severity does each response engage |
| Contingent actions | What the bank can actually do, in what order, and how much each action raises |
| Data and reporting | Can the institution see its position in the detail and at the frequency each escalation level demands (reporting frequency rises with the severity of the crisis) |

Routine liquidity monitoring is a business-as-usual activity. It runs continuously regardless of whether any contingency is contemplated, and it belongs to the daily reporting suite rather than to the plan. The plan's monitoring component is narrower and different in kind: it concerns early warning indicators and escalation triggers, not the routine reporting of the daily position. Nor is routine daily reporting the same thing as the plan's data and reporting component: that component specifies the data, systems and reporting frequency the plan needs at each escalation level (and may draw on regular, possibly daily, liquidity reports), whereas the business-as-usual reporting process itself is not one of the five named components.

On the early warning indicators within the monitoring component, the factors considered are macro-environment, industry and institution-specific measures. A generic 'financial measures' category is not one of them, because every one of the three named categories is expressed through financial measures.

decisions.final:
The characteristics of an effective intraday liquidity risk governance structure and why intraday exposure belongs inside the wider risk framework.

The reading lists four characteristics of an effective governance structure; option B names three of them, and no other option is consistent with any of them.

| Characteristic | What it requires |
|---|---|
| Active risk management | Intraday liquidity risk is actively managed rather than accepted as a cost of doing business: settlement and systemic risks are classified in the firm's risk taxonomy and incorporated into its risk appetite framework |
| Risk assessment | Intraday liquidity risk is treated as a component of the firm's risk self-assessments |
| Integration with risk governance | The three lines of defence: treasury (first line), risk management (second line) and internal audit (third line) |
| Risk measurement and monitoring | The amount of intraday credit the institution extends to clients, and the amount of intraday credit it uses itself |

Why integration matters. The tempting view is that an exposure extinguished by the close is not a real exposure. It is: a bank that cannot meet a settlement obligation at two in the afternoon has failed, regardless of what its end-of-day balance sheet would have shown. Intraday liquidity is also the channel through which a clearing bank's withdrawal of credit can halt a dealer's activity within a single day, which is one of the named failure mechanisms.

The operations-only framing fails for the same reason. Intraday exposure is created by business decisions, such as which clients receive intraday credit lines and how large the securities settlement book is, so governance has to reach the functions that make those decisions.
